negative-feedback.title: The error is not zero
negative-feedback.prompt: A noninverting forward block has gain A = 2000 and feedback fraction b = 0.05. For a 50 mV input, find loop gain, closed-loop gain, output and error.
negative-feedback.hint: Solve y = A(x − by), then check A times the error.

solution.text: A × e = 0.99010 V confirms the result. Output is slightly below the ideal 1 V because finite forward gain requires a nonzero error.

negative-feedback.title: A parameter change, twice
negative-feedback.prompt: A = 1000 and b = 0.1. Estimate the percentage gain change for a small 2% increase in A. Then calculate the exact change if A doubles.
negative-feedback.hint: Use differential sensitivity for the small change; recalculate G for the large change.

solution.text: Doubling A changes G from 1000/101 = 9.90099 to 2000/201 = 9.95025, an increase of about 0.4975%. The original derivative times 100% is not the correct finite-change calculation.

negative-feedback.title: Two disturbances with different outcomes
negative-feedback.prompt: A = 1000, b = 0.1. Find output change due to a 0.2 V disturbance added at the output inside the sensing point. Compare a +1 mV error added to the returned measurement before subtraction.
negative-feedback.hint: Write y = A(x − by − n) + d.

solution.text: Output disturbance is suppressed. Measurement error is interpreted as a true output change and produces a correction of nearly −n/b.

negative-feedback.title: A single-pole calculation
negative-feedback.prompt: An amplifier has A₀ = 5000 and its only pole at 20 Hz. With b = 0.02, find closed-loop DC gain and pole frequency.

solution.text: The product is 100 kHz, the same as A₀fp. Extra poles, large-signal slew limits and loading can invalidate this one-pole tradeoff.

negative-feedback.title: Where to read the phase
negative-feedback.prompt: A conventional stable open-loop system has one unity loop-gain crossover at 8 kHz. Its loop phase there is −135°. What is phase margin? Is phase at the signal amplifier’s −3 dB point the right substitute?
negative-feedback.hint: The critical phase condition is −180° at unity loop magnitude.

solution.text: No. The relevant crossover is |A b| = 1, not the closed-loop signal response’s −3 dB point. General multi-crossover or open-loop-unstable systems require additional stability analysis.

transistor-feedback.title: Include the junction resistance
transistor-feedback.prompt: At IC = 1 mA, VT = 25.85 mV, β = 100, RC = 2.2 kΩ and RE = 100 Ω, find midband base-to-collector gain and base input resistance. Ignore Early effect and loading.
transistor-feedback.hint: Use gm = IC/VT and keep the finite denominator.

solution.text: The limiting resistor ratio would give −22 and is not yet accurate at this loop gain.

transistor-feedback.title: Choose the unbypassed resistor
transistor-feedback.prompt: For the same 1 mA, β = 100 transistor and effective collector resistance 2.2 kΩ, calculate RE for a base-to-collector gain of −10.
transistor-feedback.hint: Rearrange the exact degeneration gain expression.

solution.text: This sets the small-signal gain under the stated assumptions. Bias, load, source attenuation and usable output swing still need separate checks.

transistor-feedback.title: A unity target with finite loop gain
transistor-feedback.prompt: At IC = 1 mA and β = 100, an emitter follower has an effective emitter load of 1 kΩ. Find its base-to-emitter gain. With source resistance 1 kΩ and an actual 1 kΩ emitter resistor, estimate unloaded output resistance.
transistor-feedback.hint: Use ge = gm(1 + 1/β), then reflect the source/base resistance into the emitter.

solution.text: The AC voltage gain is near one, but DC emitter voltage still differs from base by VBE. Output resistance worsens as the base source becomes less stiff.

transistor-feedback.title: Do not forget base current in RC
transistor-feedback.prompt: A collector-to-base bias circuit has VCC = 12 V, VBE = 0.7 V, RC = 2.2 kΩ, RF = 220 kΩ and β = 100. No external DC base current flows. Find IB, IC and VC.
transistor-feedback.hint: The collector resistor supplies IC + IB.

solution.text: The transistor remains forward-active in this first model because the collector is well above the base. A directly connected signal source could change the DC equation.

transistor-feedback.title: Follow the signs and the disturbance
transistor-feedback.prompt: Two loaded common-emitter stages have gains −15 and −40. An ideal return network applies 0.1 of the final output to the first emitter. Find closed-loop gain and the response to a 0.3 V disturbance added at the output inside the pickup.
transistor-feedback.hint: Two inversions make the forward gain positive; raising the first emitter subtracts input.

solution.text: These are static loaded-block results. The real feedback network and both stage poles must be included before making a stability claim.

regulated-supplies.title: Finite loop gain in a supply
regulated-supplies.prompt: A 1.2 V reference and divider with 30 kΩ top / 10 kΩ bottom drive a forward gain of 800. Find ideal and finite-gain unloaded outputs.

solution.text: The finite-gain shortfall is 1/201 = 0.4975%. Reference and resistor-ratio errors would be additional.

regulated-supplies.title: A transistor current limiter
regulated-supplies.prompt: Design a nominal 250 mA current limiter using an assumed sensing VBE of 0.6 V. Find sense resistance and its dissipation at the limit. A pass transistor has β = 40 at that load; estimate required base current.
regulated-supplies.hint: The sense resistor is part of the voltage and power budget.

solution.text: VBE variation changes the current threshold. The 0.6 V sensing drop also consumes headroom, and the driver needs its own current margin.

regulated-supplies.title: A current-limited short
regulated-supplies.prompt: A supply may see 15 V input and normally provides 5 V at 200 mA. Its short-circuit current remains 200 mA. Find normal and shorted pass dissipation. With 40 °C ambient and 110 °C design junction target, find maximum total thermal resistance for the sustained short.
regulated-supplies.hint: Current limiting controls current, not necessarily temperature.

solution.tex: P_{normal}=2\ \mathrm W,\quad P_{short}=3\ \mathrm W,\quad\theta_{total}\leq70/3=23.33\ ^\circ\mathrm C/\mathrm W

solution.text: Check transistor DC safe operating area as well as this heat-flow estimate. A power rating alone does not establish safety at simultaneous high VCE and IC.

regulated-supplies.title: Before feedback catches up
regulated-supplies.prompt: A 150 mA load step is initially supplied by a 220 µF output capacitor. Controller response takes 30 µs and ESR is 0.08 Ω. Estimate capacitive droop and immediate ESR drop.
regulated-supplies.hint: Treat current as constant during the short interval.

solution.text: A rough combined early drop is 32.45 mV, before wiring inductance and the detailed loop response. The capacitor also affects loop stability.

regulated-supplies.title: A high average is not enough
regulated-supplies.prompt: A 5 V regulator needs 1 V of input headroom. Its rectified input has 7 V mean and 2.4 V peak-to-peak ripple, approximately symmetric about the mean. Can it remain regulated throughout the cycle?
regulated-supplies.hint: Compare the trough with the required input, not the mean.

solution.text: No. It enters dropout near the trough despite a 7 V mean. Reduce ripple, lower the required headroom or increase minimum raw voltage, then recheck maximum-voltage heating.

temperature-control.title: Power and time are different budgets
temperature-control.prompt: A body has θ = 8 °C/W and Cth = 25 J/°C. Ambient is 20 °C and target is 60 °C. Find required holding power and time constant. Is a 4 W heater sufficient?
temperature-control.hint: Use equilibrium heat loss and thermal energy storage separately.

solution.text: A 4 W heater is insufficient: its ideal equilibrium is only 52 °C. No feedback gain can overcome that actuator limit.

temperature-control.title: The error commands the holding power
temperature-control.prompt: A proportional temperature controller has Kp = 0.5 W/°C, θ = 10 °C/W, target 50 °C and ambient 20 °C. Find equilibrium temperature, error and power.
temperature-control.hint: Equate commanded power to heat loss.

solution.tex: e=30/(1+10(0.5))=5\ ^\circ\mathrm C,\quad T=45\ ^\circ\mathrm C,\quad P=2.5\ \mathrm W

solution.text: If error were zero, a pure proportional controller would command zero power. An integral or feedforward term can retain a nonzero holding command at zero error.

temperature-control.title: An NTC can reverse the sign you expect
temperature-control.prompt: A 10 kΩ-at-25 °C NTC with B = 3950 K is the lower leg of a 5 V divider with a 10 kΩ upper resistor. Estimate its resistance and sensor voltage at 50 °C. Should a cold sensor produce more or less heater drive?
temperature-control.hint: Use kelvin in the exponential. The lower resistor decreases as temperature rises.

solution.text: Cold means larger resistance and larger sensor voltage. A controller using sensor voltage minus target-sensor voltage should increase heating when that error is positive.

temperature-control.title: Check the cubic condition
temperature-control.prompt: A thermal plant has τ = 200 s, θ = 10 °C/W, sensor lag τs = 50 s and Kp = 0.5 W/°C. In the unsaturated linear model, what upper bound on positive Ki follows from the cubic Routh condition?

solution.text: Equality is the marginal boundary for this restricted model; a practical design needs margin. Saturation and sensor nonlinearities are not included in the criterion.

temperature-control.title: Heat in the wrong place
temperature-control.prompt: A 12 V source drives a 24 Ω heater through a BJT in linear mode at 250 mA. Find heater voltage/power and transistor dissipation. If the transistor is not thermally attached to the controlled body, how much of the electrical power enters the heater?

solution.text: Only the heater’s 1.5 W is deposited there in this model. The source supplies 3 W; the transistor dissipates the other half elsewhere. Include its SOA and cooling separately.

bjt-logic.title: Truth does not guarantee voltage
bjt-logic.prompt: A diode AND gate uses a 10 kΩ pull-up to 5 V. One input is held at 0.2 V and the conducting diode drops 0.7 V. Find output voltage and current sunk by the LOW input. Would a receiver requiring LOW below 0.8 V necessarily accept it?
bjt-logic.hint: The LOW input clamps output one diode drop above itself.

solution.text: No: 0.9 V exceeds the specified 0.8 V LOW limit. A correct Boolean function is insufficient without compatible electrical levels.

bjt-logic.title: Size the base resistor
bjt-logic.prompt: A 5 V NPN inverter has RC = 2.2 kΩ. Assume VOL = 0.2 V, VBE = 0.7 V and choose a forced-β target no greater than 10. Find the maximum base resistor with a 5 V input.
bjt-logic.hint: Calculate required collector current before base drive.

solution.text: An 18 kΩ nominal choice supplies about 0.239 mA and gives forced β ≈ 9.13 without additional collector loading. Add tolerances and actual device saturation specifications.

bjt-logic.title: Why one following gate can fail the budget
bjt-logic.prompt: A DTL NAND output has 0.257 mA base current, a 2.2 kΩ collector pull-up to 5 V and assumed 0.2 V LOW. Each following input requires 0.41 mA when LOW. Under a forced-β ≤ 10 target, is even one following input supported?
bjt-logic.hint: Subtract the gate’s own pull-up current from the allowed collector current.

solution.text: No: 0.388 mA is less than 0.41 mA. This does not prove a particular transistor cannot work; it means the chosen conservative design calculation does not guarantee the assumed LOW level.

bjt-logic.title: Check both logic levels
bjt-logic.prompt: A driver guarantees VOH ≥ 4.0 V and VOL ≤ 0.3 V. A receiver requires VIH ≥ 2.8 V or VIL ≤ 1.0 V. Find HIGH and LOW noise margins.
bjt-logic.hint: Subtract the guaranteed output boundary from the relevant input boundary in the proper direction.

solution.text: These margins require the driver specifications to hold under the actual load and supply conditions. Undefined intermediate input voltages are not a third guaranteed logic state.

bjt-logic.title: A weaker pull-up is slower
bjt-logic.prompt: A collector output rises through 4.7 kΩ into 100 pF, starting at 0.2 V and approaching 5 V. Find the time to cross 2.8 V. Ignore transistor storage time.
bjt-logic.hint: Solve the exponential charging equation for the threshold time.

solution.text: Storage time and other parasitics can add delay. The resistor change that improves LOW-state fan-out can simultaneously worsen HIGH-state speed.
